name: Crowhurst Yew

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database (Tim Hills 1997 to 2004 survey, Peter Norton re-measurements)

access: Free. It stands in the public churchyard of St George's, in the care of the parish church. No ticket or gate fee.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the low door, four feet high, in its hollow trunk, and by the chains and props. It stands east-north-east of St George's church, near the east end.
story:
Around 1820 the vicar of Crowhurst had a door fitted to this yew and put a bench and a table inside it. The hollow was said to seat ten to fourteen people, and in 1825 the Stamford Mercury reported a choir singing in there.

The tree held a stranger surprise. A seven-pound cannonball was found in or embedded in the trunk, supposed to date from the Civil War, though nobody can say how it got there.

Crowhurst's paper trail starts unusually early. A parish record says the yew was ten yards round in the time of Charles I, which is about 9.1 metres. The Ancient Yew Group's survey taped it at 10.03 metres at about four feet up in 1999, and a re-measurement in 2013 gave the same figure. Under a metre in nearly four centuries, if the old yards can be trusted.

It has paid for its fame. The roof of the hollow had fallen in by 1850. The 1999 survey found two gaps in the bole, much dead wood, a chain swallowed by new growth and the door, four feet high, still in place. A photograph from September 2024 shows it alive.

Nobody has dated it. The survey treats yews of seven metres and more as probably over 800 years old, an estimate from size alone. The earliest parts of St George's are 12th century.
transport: Crowhurst has no station. Lingfield station is about 4 km to the south in a straight line and Hurst Green about 4 km to the north, both further by lane. Check Traveline for buses.

name: Tandridge Yew

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database (Tim Hills 1997 to 2004 survey, Peter Norton re-measurements)

access: Free. It stands in the public churchyard of St Peter's, Tandridge, in the care of the parish church. No ticket or gate fee.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the huge hollow, split trunk mass under a vast spreading crown, with younger yews growing around it. It stands at the west end of St Peter's church.
story:
This yew was reported dying in 1831, and again in 1850. Sources from 1936 and 1958 describe a tree that had recovered strongly, and a photograph from 2021 shows it still standing at the west end of St Peter's.

How big it is depends on where you hold the tape. The Ancient Yew Group's survey recorded 10.92 metres in 1999, but that figure was taken five centimetres off the ground, around a fluted, split mass of several stems, so it is not a trunk measurement in the usual sense. Taken five feet up, older figures run from about 30 feet in 1850 to between 32 and 37 feet across the years 1880 to 1999.

The main stem fractured long ago, leaving two great lateral trunks that an 1890 account measured at 10 feet and 13 feet 4 inches. The cavity inside is darkened by fire or smoke. It is tall as well as stout, with many straight fluted branches, and a 1936 source gave the circle of its canopy as 250 feet.

The younger yews around it were probably layered from the parent, which would make this a small family gathered round one wreck. The size class puts it at probably over 800 years, an estimate and not a date. The earliest parts of the church are Norman.
transport: Oxted station is about 2.5 km to the north-east in a straight line, further by lane. Check Traveline for buses.

name: Wilmington Yew

location.address: St Mary and St Peter's Church, Wilmington, East Sussex

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database (Tim Hills 1997 to 2004 survey, Peter Norton re-measurements)

access: Free. It stands in the public churchyard of St Mary and St Peter, Wilmington, in the care of the parish church. No ticket or gate fee.

location_site.name: St Mary and St Peter's Church churchyard

how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the two big hollow trunks leaning in opposite directions from one massive base, held by props and chains. It stands north of the church of St Mary and St Peter.
story:
In 1850 a villager aged 85 said this yew had not changed in the 75 years they had known it. The Sussex Archaeological Collections printed the remark that year and called the tree one of the greatest antiquities of the place.

It looks like two trees and is counted as one. Two hollow, fluted trunks, each about 16 feet round in 1999, slant apart in opposite directions from a single massive base. A 1997 Sussex tree book described them as the healed halves of a single stem, and the common base is why the Ancient Yew Group's survey gives one figure for the pair, 9.15 metres. A dictionary of 1848 had it at six yards round at two feet up.

The halves no longer manage alone. Props and chains hold them, under a spreading, windswept crown. The survey was back to re-measure in 2015, the newest dated record of it.

Nobody has dated the tree. Yews of seven metres and more are classed as probably over 800 years old, which is an estimate from girth and nothing firmer, and a twin stem makes even that loose. North of it stands a 12th-century church, and above both, cut into the hillside, the Long Man of Wilmington.
transport: Berwick station, on the line between Lewes and Eastbourne, is about 3 km to the north-west in a straight line. Check Traveline for buses.

name: Corhampton Yew

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database (Tim Hills 1997 to 2004 survey, Peter Norton re-measurements)

access: Free. It stands in the public churchyard of Corhampton Church, in the care of the parish church. No ticket or gate fee.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the clean, tall bole and the big branches that reach across the path and root in the ground, with one prop left. It stands in the churchyard of the Saxon church at Corhampton.
story:
The church beside this yew owns its portrait. An early 18th-century watercolour is the earliest record of the tree, and travel writers were praising it again in 1865 and 1897.

It is a tall female with an unusually clean bole, and it has spread far past the trunk. Big branches reach across the churchyard path and take root where they touch the ground. A large leading branch and a second one divide at about seven feet. Fifteen props once held the crown up. One remains.

The measurements are close to one another for once, 7.32 metres near the ground in 1998 and 7.16 metres at 1.4 metres up in 2011. That 2011 re-measurement is the newest dated evidence we have, so a recent photograph would be welcome. Foliage was healthy and green when the Ancient Yew Group's survey saw it in 1999.

The church is a late Saxon building, founded in 1020 on an artificial mound, and it has no dedication to any saint. Its age is documented. The tree's is not. At this size the survey's girth class says probably over 800 years, which is an estimate, and only just inside the class at that.
transport: No railway in the Meon Valley. Corhampton is on the A32 between Alton and Fareham; check Traveline for buses.

name: Stedham Yew

location.address: St James's Church, Stedham, West Sussex

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database (Tim Hills 1997 to 2004 survey, Peter Norton re-measurements)

access: Free. It stands in the public churchyard of St James's, Stedham, in the care of the parish church. No ticket or gate fee.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the hollow, outward-leaning trunk with old steel wire sunk into the wood, and a big crown pouring from the top. It stands south-west of St James's church.
story:
Stedham's yew has swallowed the steel wire that was put in to hold it together. The wire is now enveloped in new wood, and the dead timber crossing the hollow has been grown over as well.

It has been hollow for at least two centuries. An account of 1815 called it a very remarkable yew of great height, 28 feet round a yard up, hollow, with a flourishing head. The figures since then barely stir: 28 feet 6 inches in 1880, 28 feet in 1952, 29 feet 6 inches at the ground when the Ancient Yew Group's survey came in 1999, and 29 feet 5 inches in January 2012. The heights differ and the tape ran over an undulating base, so treat them as neighbours and not as a growth curve. A 1997 record gives its height as 11 metres.

The trunk leans outward, and branches pour from the top of the bole. It grows south-west of St James's, whose tower is dated 1673 and which keeps one Norman-looking window.

The survey classes yews of seven metres and more as probably over 800 years old. That is an estimate from girth, and no one has dated this one. The newest dated evidence we have is from 2012, so if you go, tell us how it looks.
transport: No railway. Stedham is just west of Midhurst, off the A272; check Traveline for buses.

name: Dunsfold Yew

location.address: St Mary and All Saints' Church, Dunsfold, Surrey

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database (Tim Hills 1997 to 2004 survey, Peter Norton re-measurements)

access: Free. It stands in the public churchyard of St Mary and All Saints, Dunsfold, in the care of the parish church. No ticket or gate fee.

location_site.name: St Mary and All Saints' Church churchyard

how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the hollow trunk filled in with concrete, with new growth from several points. It stands close to the south porch of St Mary and All Saints; a small yew tunnel forms the churchyard entrance.
story:
At some point somebody filled this yew with concrete. The evidence is there in the hollow trunk beside the south porch of St Mary and All Saints, and the Ancient Yew Group's survey worried that the weight was bearing on the tree.

It seems to have carried on regardless. Growth from six separate places suggests the old trunk is renewing itself. The Victoria County History of 1911 called it probably one of the most ancient trees in the county, and that was a century before the survey arrived.

The number on site belongs to a plaque, and the plaque is on a different tree. A newer yew nearby states that a yew has stood near the door for 700 years. We have no date for either.

The tape reads steadily. It was 23 feet round in 1903, 24 feet 6 inches at three feet up in 1955, 7.52 metres just above the ground in 1998, and 24 feet 8 inches near the ground in 2013. That last visit is the newest dated evidence we have. At this girth the survey's class suggests probably over 800 years, an estimate and no more.

The church is 13th century, and the way into its churchyard is a small tunnel of yew.
transport: Witley station is about 6 km to the north-west in a straight line, further by lane. Check Traveline for buses.

name: Charlwood Yew

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database (Tim Hills 1997 to 2004 survey, Peter Norton re-measurements)

access: Free. It stands in the public churchyard of St Nicholas's, Charlwood, in the care of the parish church. No ticket or gate fee.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the single large hollowed trunk, its shell open through a gap four feet wide and blackened by fire inside. It stands south-east of St Nicholas's church.
story:
An account of 1850 dismissed this as a decayed yew-tree. It was still growing 163 years later, when the last dated measurement was taken.

Decayed is fair. It is a hollow shell with slivers of new wood inside, its inner walls badly burned, open through a gap four feet wide that was once netted with wire. In 2013 the foliage was sparse on the west side and healthy on the east, a tree alive on one flank.

A 1936 guide, The King's England, gave it 28 feet round. The Ancient Yew Group's survey judged that a mistake, and its own tape read 23 feet 8 inches in 1999 and 23 feet 5 inches in 2013. Those are 7.21 and 7.14 metres, close to the line where the survey's class says probably over 800 years. It is an estimate from size, and a shell this damaged makes any size hard to read.

It grows south-east of St Nicholas's, a church built about 1080, in a churchyard inside a conservation area. The newest dated evidence for the tree is that 2013 visit, so a current photograph would be useful.
transport: Gatwick Airport station is about 5 km to the east in a straight line, further by road. Check Traveline for buses.

name: Coldwaltham Yew

location.address: St Giles's Church, Coldwaltham, West Sussex

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database (Tim Hills 1997 to 2004 survey, Peter Norton re-measurements)

access: Free. It stands in the public churchyard of St Giles's, Coldwaltham, in the care of the parish church. No ticket or gate fee.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the very large, completely hollow bole with two straight fluted branches rising from it, and a notice naming it among the oldest yews. It stands north-west of St Giles's church.
story:
A gazetteer once gave this yew 3,000 years, and the Ancient Yew Group calls that figure unsupported. A notice at the tree claims a place among the twelve oldest yews, which the group says is possible but unlisted. A published book on the trees of Sussex goes a step less far and regards it as the county's senior veteran yew.

The measured facts are impressive enough. It was 10.49 metres round fifteen centimetres off the ground in 1999, 34 feet 5 inches by the tape. A second visit in 2012 got the identical 34 feet 5 inches, and 30 feet 9 inches at three feet up. A 1997 record makes it 14 metres tall.

Inside there is nothing left. It is completely hollow, with major cavities at the base, and many nails have been hammered into the bole over the years. Two straight fluted branches rise from what remains, a central branch is closing around old growth, and one large limb has been removed. It is a female.

The crown was thinner in 2012 than in 1999, and 2012 is the newest dated evidence we have. If you go, tell us how it looks. By the survey's girth class it is probably over 800 years old, an estimate from size. The Norman church beside it was rebuilt in the 19th century.
transport: Pulborough station is about 3 km to the north-east in a straight line, further by road. Check Traveline for buses.

name: Tangmere Yew

location.address: St Andrew's Church, Tangmere, West Sussex

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database (Tim Hills 1997 to 2004 survey, Peter Norton re-measurements)

access: Free. It stands in the public churchyard of St Andrew's, Tangmere, in the care of the parish church. No ticket or gate fee.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the stout trunk of a female yew and the leaning section held by chains that carries the main branch. It stands south of St Andrew's church.
story:
In the 1760s this yew was declared dead, and another was planted to take its place. The replacement failed. The old yew recovered.

Eighty years later it had an audience. The Illustrated London News featured it in February 1846, and in 1885 the Church Builder called it the finest in all the country round. It had been measured at 20 feet at a yard up in 1848, and by 1988 the same height gave 24 feet 8 inches. A re-measurement in 2011 found 24 feet 4 inches at three feet. A yew that loses four inches in 23 years says more about tapes than about yews. Lower down the trunk's growth distorts every reading. The Ancient Yew Group's survey recorded 8.08 metres at 30 centimetres in 1999.

It is a female, 12 metres tall in a 1997 record, and the survey called it a fine healthy one. A leaning section held by chains carries the main branch, and new wood is being laid down on the inner surface, a slow way of rebuilding from within.

The girth class says probably over 800 years, an estimate rather than a date. A Saxon church here was replaced about 1100. The newest dated evidence for the tree is 2011, so an up-to-date photograph would be welcome.
transport: Chichester station is about 5 km to the west-south-west in a straight line, further by road. Tangmere lies just north of the A27; check Traveline for buses.

name: Itchen Abbas Yew

location.address: St John the Baptist's Church, Itchen Abbas, Hampshire

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database (Tim Hills 1997 to 2004 survey, Peter Norton re-measurements)

access: Free. It stands in the public churchyard of St John the Baptist, Itchen Abbas, in the care of the parish church. No ticket or gate fee.

location_site.name: St John the Baptist's Church churchyard

how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the gnarled trunk with huge side limbs removed and a reduced crown, graves around its base. It stands east of the church on the mound beside the River Itchen, not the smaller male on the porch path.
story:
A book of 1994 says this yew is recorded in a Saxon charter of 939. We have not seen that charter or a transcript of it, so treat it as a claim. If it holds, the tree is more than a thousand years old.

The evidence we can stand on is newer and closer to hand. The Ancient Yew Group's survey measured 7.77 metres at 45 centimetres in April 1999, and the group has been back repeatedly since, in 2010, 2011, from 2017 to 2019, and in 2023 and 2024. Its written history in the group's files runs from 1839.

The last visit found it in fairly good condition, though the tree is not the shape it was. Huge side limbs have been removed, the lower branches are hollow, and the crown is lower than it appears in old photographs. It stands on a mound east of the church, beside the River Itchen. Another yew, a male of nine feet at one foot up, stands on the path to the porch.

The church has late 11th-century origins and a Victorian present. The tree's own age is not recorded. The survey's size class says probably over 800 years, an estimate from girth that neither confirms the charter nor rules it out.
transport: Winchester station is about 6 km to the south-west in a straight line, further by road. Itchen Abbas is on the B3047; check Traveline for buses.
